items.definition: Fossil (conventional) fuels are organic fuels extracted from underground deposits that formed naturally from decayed plant matter over millions of years; they are built from hydrogen-and-carbon molecules, hence the name hydrocarbons.
items.core_idea: Organic fuels supply the overwhelming majority of world energy, and are split into fossil fuels (ancient, extracted from the ground) versus biofuels (produced from recently grown crops).
key_points: Organic-source fuels supply more than 90% of world energy.
Fossil fuels form over millions of years from trapped, decaying plant life.
Biofuels are the same broad hydrocarbon category but sourced from recently grown crops rather than ancient underground deposits.
Burning (combusting) hydrocarbons with oxygen releases heat used to power engines or generators.
relationships: Fossil fuels and biofuels are both hydrocarbon fuels, distinguished by the age/source of the organic material rather than chemical composition.
common_misunderstandings: Fossil fuel and hydrocarbon are not strict synonyms — hydrocarbon is the chemical category, while fossil fuel specifies the ancient-underground origin as opposed to biofuel.

items.topic: Exploration and production as two distinct activities
items.definition: Before fossil fuels can be sold, they must be located (exploration) and then physically extracted from the ground (production), typically by a specialized company working with the mineral rights owner.
items.core_idea: Exploration covers licensing, searching for resources, and negotiating extraction contracts with mineral rights owners; production covers the physical extraction via drilling (oil/gas) or mining (coal).
key_points: Exploration = getting search licenses, locating resources, and negotiating contracts with mineral rights owners.
Production = extracting the fuel, via drilling for oil and gas or mining for coal.
After production, fuels must be separated from each other via refining before being sold to consumers.
This work is often performed by a dedicated exploration and production (E&P) company rather than the mineral rights owner directly.
relationships: Production precedes refining, which precedes consumer sale.

items.topic: Hydrocarbon classification by carbon chain length
items.definition: Hydrocarbon fuels are categorized by the length of their carbon chain, notated Cn where n is the number of carbon atoms; chain length determines whether the fuel is a gas, liquid, or solid at standard temperature and pressure.
items.core_idea: Short carbon chains form natural gas (gaseous), mid-length chains form petroleum (liquid), and the longest chains form coal (solid).
key_points: Carbon-chain notation: capital C plus a subscript for the number of carbon atoms, e.g. C5 = five-carbon molecule.
Shortest chains (natural gases) are gaseous at standard temperature and pressure.
Mid-length chains (petroleum) are liquid.
Longest chains (coal) are solid.

Even after processing, fuels remain mixtures of hydrocarbons of varying chain length rather than a single pure molecule — e.g. gasoline is predominantly C7–C11 but also contains some C5, C6, C12, C13, etc.

The proportion of lighter/heavier molecules in a fuel like gasoline can vary substantially, so the carbon-chain makeup of a named fuel (e.g. 'gasoline') may be defined slightly differently across countries, states, or even processing locations.
relationships: Carbon chain length is the underlying variable linking natural gas, petroleum, and coal as points on one spectrum rather than unrelated substances.
trading_implications: Because named fuel grades (e.g. gasoline) are regionally-defined mixtures rather than fixed chemical formulas, specification differences across jurisdictions can matter for physical delivery/quality contracts.
common_misunderstandings: Natural gas, petroleum, and coal are not chemically distinct categories in an absolute sense — they are ranges along a continuous carbon-chain-length spectrum.

items.topic: Mineral rights ownership and licensing for E&P
items.definition: Energy companies lease land to extract fuel and compensate both the surface land owner and the mineral rights owner (often the same or different parties) via royalties, a share of production profit; who owns subsurface mineral rights varies by country.
items.core_idea: In the U.S., subsurface fossil fuel rights are commonly privately owned, whereas in most other countries they belong to the government; regardless of ownership, exploration companies must obtain licenses first to explore and then, separately, to develop identified resources for production.
key_points: Producers pay royalties — a percentage of production profit — to land and mineral rights owners.
U.S.: subsurface fossil fuel rights are often privately owned.
Most other countries: subsurface resources are government-owned.
Two licensing stages: one to explore for new resources, a separate one to develop/produce once resources are identified.
relationships: Royalty-based compensation connects to the Tax and Royalty contract structure described later in the same section.
common_misunderstandings: Ownership of surface land does not automatically imply ownership of subsurface mineral rights, and the two can be held by different parties.

items.definition: A landman is a professional who negotiates land titles and mineral leases on behalf of an oil and gas exploration company.
items.core_idea: Landmen identify and contact potential land/mineral-rights sellers on behalf of an exploration company and then negotiate the resulting lease or purchase contracts.
key_points: Landmen act as the exploration company's representative for identifying willing sellers of mineral rights.
They also handle negotiation of the resulting contracts once a willing owner is found.
related_topics: Mineral rights ownership and licensing for E&P

items.definition: E&P is potentially very profitable but carries significant risk at several stages: technical/mechanical failure during extraction, leasing land that turns out to have no economically extractable reserves, and the risk that future price declines make previously-profitable reserves unprofitable after wells are already drilled.
items.core_idea: Risk in E&P is multi-layered — technical execution risk, resource/geological risk (no viable reserves found), and price risk that can turn a good discovery bad after capital has already been committed.
key_points: Technical complexity means mechanical problems can arise even when a project is otherwise going well.
A company can take a lease and find no identifiable fuel reserves at all.
A company can identify real reserves that are nonetheless uneconomic to extract.
Even initially profitable reserves can become unprofitable if energy prices fall after wells have already been drilled — i.e., risk persists after the sunk investment.
Because of this uncertainty, a variety of contract structures exist to allocate risk between the exploration company and the resource owner.
relationships: This risk landscape motivates the different contract types (tax and royalty, production sharing, service contract) that allocate risk differently between developer and owner.
trading_implications: Price risk is not limited to the point of initial investment decision — a project judged profitable at the time of drilling can become unprofitable purely due to subsequent price moves, independent of execution quality.

items.definition: A contract structure where the exploration company (developer) pays the mineral rights owner an up-front licensing fee plus a percentage of gross profits (a typical U.S. figure cited is one-eighth of gross profits).
items.core_idea: Under a tax and royalty contract, the developer bears essentially all of the development risk while the owner is shielded from out-of-pocket losses, though both parties are exposed to the effect of falling energy prices on profit share.
key_points: Owner receives an up-front fee plus a percentage of gross profits.
A typical U.S. royalty share cited is one-eighth of gross profits.
The exploration company bears essentially all development risk.
The mineral rights owner never has to pay out of pocket — their downside is limited to reduced profits, not losses.
Both developer and owner are still exposed to declining energy prices reducing the profit pool.
relationships: Contrasts with production sharing (owner takes more risk for potentially higher reward) and service contracts (developer takes no ownership stake at all).
trading_implications: This is the lowest-risk structure for the mineral rights owner among the three described, at the cost of lower potential upside compared to production sharing.
related_topics: Mineral rights ownership and licensing for E&P

items.definition: A contract structure where the exploration company gives the mineral rights owner a share of the physical fuel produced (rather than a cash royalty), leaving the owner responsible for selling or using that fuel.
items.core_idea: Because the owner takes on the additional burden and risk of handling and marketing physical fuel themselves, a production sharing contract can yield the owner higher profits than a tax and royalty contract, but requires the owner to have the knowledge and capability to transact in physical energy.
key_points: Owner receives a percentage of the physical fuel produced, not a cash royalty.
Owner must independently arrange to sell or use that fuel, requiring physical energy transaction capability.
Owner bears more risk than under a tax and royalty contract, which can translate into higher potential profit.
relationships: Sits between tax and royalty (lower owner risk/reward) and full risk-bearing on the spectrum of E&P contract structures.
trading_implications: Owners choosing production sharing take on commodity marketing/sales risk in addition to production-side risk, which only makes sense if they have the operational capacity to handle physical fuel.

items.definition: A contract structure where the developer acts purely as a paid contractor to produce oil and gas for a fee, without taking ownership of the crude oil produced.
items.core_idea: Under a service contract the developer is compensated as a fee-for-service provider rather than as a profit-or-loss stakeholder in the extracted fuel itself.
key_points: Developer is paid a fee to produce oil and gas.
Developer does not take ownership of the crude oil produced.
relationships: Represents the lowest-risk-for-developer end of the E&P contract spectrum, contrasted with tax and royalty and production sharing where the developer/owner take on production or price risk.
